title: When should I start talking to kids about money?
content:
## **When to Talk to Kids About Money!**



Here is a secret: you are already talking to and teaching kids about money, and so is the world. 

**However,*italic text*** "you" are most likely not doing it intentionally!!! 

That is a **GARGANTUAN** of a problem for kids and their long term financial wellness. 

So, **starting today**, let's begin addressing the challenge, solving the problem, and getting children on the path to financial freedom and security.


Most children don't learn about money until it's too late to build real habits. At Grow Good Daily, we believe starting financial education at age 3 changes everything and the research backs us up.

If you've ever handed your child a dollar at the school fair and watched them spend it on the first shiny thing they saw, you're not alone. Many parents wait until the "right moment" to talk about money until kids are old enough to understand, responsible enough to care, or old enough to have a job. But here's the truth: by the time that moment feels right, the habits are already forming without you.

Kids are always learning about money, often unconsciously and unintentionally. It is unavoidable.

Financial habits, the emotional relationship particularly with spending, but saving, and patience as well begin developing in vert early childhood. Thus the earlier you choose to take care of your child's financial education with
gentle, age-appropriate conversations about money, the better equipped your child will be for life.

Research from the University of Cambridge found that adult money habits and attitudes are largely formed by age 7. 

Take a few seconds to digest that. It will be a game changer for you and your children if you are able to do so and act on it. 

What it means is the window between ages 3 and 7 is a critical, to set your children up for a lifetime of financial wellness that includes more peace of mind, security, and opportunities. 

Unfortunately it is far to frequently a missed opportunity for parents to lay the groundwork.

At age 3, children already understand the basic concept that things cost something. They've seen you tap a card, pull out a wallet, or say "we can't afford that right now." They're absorbing your relationship with money whether you're teaching them or not. The question isn't whether your children will learn about money from you. It's what they'll learn.

The Grow Good Daily Principle: Children don't need to understand interest rates or investment portfolios. They need to understand that money is a tool, something you earn, save intentionally, and choose to spend wisely. Those values take root early.

Financial education doesn't need to be a formal lesson. It's woven into everyday moments at home, in the grocery store, at the gas pump, on birthdays, etc. Here's what to focus on at each stage:

Many parents avoid money talk because they feel their own finances aren't perfect or because they weren't taught well themselves. We hear this all the time at Grow Good Daily. But here's what we've learned: you don't need to be a financial expert to raise a financially confident child. You just need to be honest and present.

Narrate your decisions out loud. "I'm choosing the store brand because it's just as good and saves us money for our vacation fund."

Let kids see and sometimes (when appropriate) join real money decisions that align to your family's values and situation.

Normalize talking about money the same way you talk about health, kindness, or hard work.

Celebrate saving, not just spending. Make piggy bank deposits a priority and source of pride, not just a slot for coins.

Correct mistakes without shame. A child who spends all their money too fast is learning, not failing. "The goal isn't to raise a child who never makes financial mistakes. It's to raise a child who has the language, values, and resilience to learn from them."

When money education is delayed or never happens intentionally kids fill the gap with what they observe and absorb at home and from culture: social media, peers, advertising. The messages they receive aren't neutral. They're designed by brands to equate spending with happiness, status, and belonging.

Young adults who never learned to save, budget, or distinguish a need from a want don't suddenly develop those skills at 18 or 22. They struggle with credit card debt, impulse spending, and a deep anxiety about finances that often lasts a lifetime.

Financial literacy isn't a subject. It's a lifelong practice  and the families who practice it together, openly and without shame, raise children who are genuinely prepared for the world.

At Grow Good Daily, we believe small daily conversations create lasting roots. Money is one of the most powerful tools your child will ever have. Help them understand it, respect it, and use it well. Start now, wherever they are, wherever you are. Because the best time to start was yesterday. The second best time? Today!
